newsitem.title: UK: LPG trade thin in Asia as Aramco acceptances high.
newsitem.headline: LPG trade thin in Asia as Aramco acceptances high.

text.p: Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) spot trade in Asia was subdued this week, dealers said.
High nomination acceptances by Saudi Aramco saw large volumes of June propane and butane loading in Yanbu for the journey east.
A trader who had nominations accepted said that seven companies received allocations for single-port loading in June from Yanbu.
Normally, he said, loading is done on a two port basis including Ras Tanura. It is rare for the allocations to be made only at Yanbu he said.
That made deliveries easier for Aramco but harder for lifters, he added.
One result of the comparatively large volumes moving east under contract in May is that the spot market was relatively quiet and was "losing direction," a dealer said.
There was still uncertainty over the level at which the Saudi Contract Price (CP), the benchmark against which Asian LPG is traded, will be set for June.
Some saw it falling $10-$15 a tonne from May, others said it may only come off around $5.
The T1 tender for June, the first of three monthly tenders which play a part in establishing the CP, was rumoured to have gone at $157 a tonne for propane and $186 a tonne for butane.
One dealer said this indicated that a fall in the CP of $10 to $15 a tonne was likely.
The tender closes on Friday, with rumours of the results expected to filter onto the market from next Tuesday.
In the North Sea, deals were done early in the week at strong numbers, lending a firmer tone to the market.
A propane cargo was done at $191 a tonne cif NWE for two-port discharge, with another was done later at $188 a tonne cif UK east coast.
But some said prices were unlikely to go much higher, as strong North Sea prices would attract Algerian material, currently concentrated on transatlantic markets.
"Things are quite tight and there's not much product around, but I don't see prices storming as otherwise Algerian will come north," he said.
A trader for Algeria's state Sonatrach confirmed that they were looking at the north, and said "if prices go up it will be attractive."
But he added that Sonatrach was still concentrating on transatlantic opportunities, with the European spot market relatively quiet.
Following the high-priced cargo deals at the beginning of the week, North Sea prices have already started to soften, with interest from petrochemical buyers seen in the low $180's a tonne.
But a trader said that non-petrochemical users who need material may still have to pay higher prices, possibly as high as $190 a tonne, leading to a wide bid/offer range.
Butane has been quiet and dull in the North Sea, with cargoes notionally talked in the high $160's or low $170's a tonne.
The main interest came from outside Europe, with some demand seen in Latin America, and there was potential seen for turning a profit by moving product outside the region.
In the Mediterranean, relative strength in the U.S. left local markets quiet as there was little interest seen.
In Lavera, propane prices were notionally assessed at $180-$190 a tonne, unchanged on a week ago.
Butane was notionally slightly weaker than propane, by between $5-$10 a tonne, also unchanged on the week.

A trader said there was some LPG interest seen from the eastern Mediterranean, especially Turkey, but with higher prices seen in northern Europe and the U.S., the local market was essentially thin and unchanged.
Towards the end of the week Norelf, the company jointly owned by subsidiaries of Enron Corp and Elf Aquitaine, said it will cease LPG trading at the end of the year.
The company said it will "maintain its active trading presence until that date." But after that, the two companies intend to remain in the LPG market as separate entities.
A Norelf source said that the two companies were competitors in other energy markets, and had decided it made sense to trade LPG as competitors rather than partners.
U.S. markets remained steady over the week, with propane at Mont Belvieu, Texas, still valued above 35 cents a gallon.

But there was some concern that high stocks in Canada may put U.S. prices under pressure. Canadian propane stocks in April were at 157 percent of their level a year ago, according to government data published in mid-week.
"Canada is swimming in propane and people are starting to worry if we aren't going to be seeing it coming our way," said one U.S. trader.
Poland was likely to double its LPG consumption to 1.2 million tonnes annually by 2000 from a current 690,000 tonnes, a conference heard this week.

Of this, 80 percent will be imported, according to Adam Kubiak, head of the Polish Liquid Gas Organisation. Average per capita consumption is around 18 kg annually, he said, compared with 30kg in western countries, but this will change as the LPG car fleet increases by 100,000 to 250,000 by 2000.
--Sebastian Alison, London Newsroom, +44 171 542 6412 (c) Reuters Limited 1997
